meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Make war a mere contest of machines without men and without loss of life'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Tesla, confirmed in the scanned original: Century Magazine, June 1900, p. 188. The quote is real; the usual truncation hides his point about peace.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Tesla wrote it himself, in “The Problem of Increasing Human Energy,” his long essay for The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine of June 1900 — the sentence sits on page 188 of the scanned issue, in the passage on his remote-controlled “telautomata.” Quote Investigator ↗ traces the line to the same article and concludes Tesla should receive the credit. One catch: the popular version stops at “loss of life,” and Tesla’s sentence does not.

source.heading: The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine, June 1900

The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine, Vol. 60, No. 2 — June 1900

source.excerpt: But the force of this new principle does not wholly reside in its destructiveness. Its advent introduces into warfare an element which never existed before—a fighting-machine without men as a means of attack and defense. The continuous development in this direction must ultimately make war a mere contest of machines without men and without loss of life—a condition which would have been impossible without this new departure, and which, in my opinion, must be reached as preliminary to permanent peace.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ examined the line in May 2019 and traced it to Tesla’s June 1900 essay in The Century Magazine (Vol. 60, No. 2), concluding that Tesla should receive credit for the words. It also records contemporary newspaper pickup of the piece — The Wichita Daily Eagle of 10 June 1900 and The San Francisco Examiner of 17 June 1900.

The wording holds up against the original object: the OCR of the scanned June 1900 issue ↗ carries “must ultimately make war a mere contest of machines without men and without loss of life” on page 188, under Tesla’s byline.
The Wikisource transcription ↗ gives the whole sentence, including the closing clause about permanent peace, and the neighbouring line “machine must fight machine.”
A Tesla archive independently hosts the essay, credited to Century Magazine, June 1900 ↗, with the surrounding passages on controlling “an individualized automaton.”
source.excerptNote: The circulating quote begins mid-sentence at “make war…” and stops at “loss of life,” dropping the clause in which Tesla explains that he considers this the precondition for permanent peace.

author.name: Nikola Tesla
author.heading: Nikola Tesla — the engineer who thought robots would end war
author.bio: Nikola Tesla (10 July 1856 – 7 January 1943) was the Serbian-American engineer, inventor and futurist behind the alternating-current induction motor and the polyphase system that carried AC power into industrial use. In 1898 he demonstrated a radio-controlled boat — a “telautomaton” — at an electrical exhibition in Madison Square Garden, and spent years arguing that such unmanned machines were less a weapon than a route out of war. He wrote for popular magazines as fluently as he filed patents, and this line comes from that side of him: the engineer as essayist, making a moral argument out of a piece of hardware.

misattribution.heading: The credit is right — the sentence is wrong
misattribution.intro: This is that rare thing among viral Tesla lines: authentic, and traceable to a page. What goes wrong is not the attribution but the wording. Two distortions travel with it.

items.who: Nikola Tesla — correctly credited, routinely truncated
items.why: The quote almost always ends at “loss of life,” which reads as a cool prophecy of robot warfare. Tesla’s sentence keeps going: the unmanned fighting machine is “a condition which… in my opinion, must be reached as preliminary to permanent peace.” Cut the clause and you invert the argument — an anti-war claim becomes a shrug about automated killing. The full sentence is in the Wikisource transcription ↗.

Versions circulate in which Tesla hopes to make war “a mere spectacle of machines” — the phrasing used on the PBS Master of Lightning companion page ↗. That fuses two separate phrases from the 1900 essay: “a mere contest of machines” in the sentence quoted here, and, several paragraphs away, turning “the battle into a mere spectacle, a play, a contest without loss of blood.” Both are Tesla’s; the hybrid is not.

misattribution.truthLine: Tesla really wrote it, in The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine for June 1900, page 188 — a conclusion reached independently by Quote Investigator ↗ and confirmable in the scanned issue itself ↗. Quote the whole sentence and you quote the man.

context.heading: Why a man who invented a war machine called it a peace plan
lead: Tesla was not celebrating mechanised slaughter — he was arguing, in his own strange way, for its abolition. In 1898 he had demonstrated a radio-controlled boat at an electrical exhibition in Madison Square Garden, a machine he called a “telautomaton,” and by 1900 he had built a whole political theory on top of it. So long as men themselves met in battle, he reasoned, there would be blood; the only way out was to take the men off the field entirely. As he put it in the same essay: machine must fight machine ↗.

That is what makes the truncated version of the quote misleading. Read whole, the sentence is a claim about peace: an unmanned fighting machine is the thing that “must be reached as preliminary to permanent peace.” Elsewhere in the article Tesla imagines the endpoint as machines meeting in a contest without bloodshed while the nations look on as “interested, ambitious spectators.” A century and a quarter of drone warfare later, the prediction has aged into something far more double-edged than its author intended.
context.detailsSummary: Where else the idea shows up in the same article
detailsBody: The June 1900 essay is a sprawling piece about harnessing energy, and the war passage arrives as a coda to Tesla’s section on telautomatics. He describes his art as a means of “absolutely controlling, in every respect, all the innumerable translatory movements” of “an individualized automaton” — the technical claim underneath the rhetorical one.

Tesla returns to the same theme in a nearby formulation, hoping to turn “the battle into a mere spectacle, a play, a contest without loss of blood.” The two phrasings are often blended together by later writers, which is how paraphrases like “a mere spectacle of machines” enter circulation. Both wordings are in the article itself ↗; neither is a substitute for the other.
